extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of 37k English multiple-choice math word problems covering multiple math domain categories, densely annotated with fully-specified operational programs in a domain-aware representation language.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset is constructed by taking problems from the AQuA dataset (Ling et al., 2017), categorizing them into math domains using term frequencies, and annotating them with operational programs via crowdsourcing, followed by annotation expansion using edit distance similarity.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Removal of unwanted noise from AQuA including unsolvable problems (problems with no words, sequence problems requiring pattern intuition, problems requiring options/brute-force enumeration, non-numeric solutions) and duplicates. Categorization into math domains using domain-specific n-gram frequencies to prune the search space of operations. Expanding annotations across closely similar problems by replacing numeric values with generic numbers using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers on Figure Eight iteratively selected mathematical operations and valid arguments (numbers from the problem, category constants, and previous calculation outputs) through a dynamic platform providing operation hints/formulas. Submissions were restricted to programs using problem numbers whose final calculation closely matched the correct numeric solution.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotator quality was controlled via test questions maintaining an accuracy threshold (untrusted annotator annotations were re-pooled). Alignment validation required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank an operation program as valid, achieving a validation accuracy of 94.64% across categories. An expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% validity and 87% agreement between expert and crowd validation.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The representation language provides supervision to reduce statistical bias; however, domain-specific categorization might introduce noise due to assigning a single mathematical interpretation to polysemous n-grams (e.g., 'square' or 'cube' indicating geometry vs. exponentiation).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset and representation language omit high-order polynomials, sequence problems, and non-numeric solutions; the representation language lacks certain operations such as factorization; problem categorization based on unigrams/n-grams can occasionally misclassify domains.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, testing, and validating neural sequence-to-program models and interpretable solvers for math word problems.
